title: I rented a car, and within hours, my driver's license was for sale
gist: A dark-web ID theft service called Nexus offered more than 153 million scanned driver's licenses (including infrared/ultraviolet spectrum images capable of defeating hologram checks), apparently sourced in near real-time from a third-party ID scanning vendor, IDScan.net, used by Hertz and other rental companies.

themes.theme: Scale and mechanism of the ID-scan breach

insights.claim: A new dark-web ID theft service called Nexus offered more than 153 million driver's licenses for sale, exposed by a KrebsOnSecurity investigation, including licenses belonging to journalist Brian Krebs, his mother, an FBI assistant director, and several security researchers.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A breach at this scale (153M+ IDs) implies systemic exposure across the ID-scanning vendor supply chain used broadly by consumer-facing businesses, not an isolated incident — relevant to cybersecurity/identity-verification vendor risk assessment.
insights.locator: An exposé published Tuesday by KrebsOnSecurity

insights.claim: The leaked ID files included not just standard image scans but also infrared and ultraviolet spectrum images of the documents, which likely enable cloned counterfeit IDs to pass hologram authenticity tests.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The presence of UV/IR scans elevates this beyond typical data breaches into enabling physical counterfeit ID production capable of bypassing standard verification — a materially higher-severity fraud/security risk.
insights.quote: the additional formats may allow cloned-based counterfeit IDs to pass hologram tests

insights.claim: The author's own driver's license scan appeared for sale on Nexus within hours of a car rental employee scanning it, indicating the breach source has near real-time access to data flowing through a third-party ID-scanning service used by rental companies.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Near-instant exposure (hours, not days) indicates an active, ongoing pipeline breach rather than a historical data dump — meaning any customer scanned by an affected vendor remains at continuous, live risk until the pipeline is secured.
insights.quote: Within hours of an employee scanning my driver's license, a high-resolution scan of my ID was available for sale on the dark web.
insights.locator: Not long ago, I rented an SUV

insights.claim: Over a 24-hour period, the number of driver's licenses listed as available on Nexus grew by almost 400,000, indicating the breach was actively ongoing rather than a one-time historical leak.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A growth rate of ~400K records/day quantifies the breach's active velocity — useful for estimating scope/duration and urgency of remediation for any exposed vendor.
insights.quote: Over a span of 24 hours, Krebs said the number of driver's licenses listed as available grew by almost 400,000.
insights.locator: The timing of newly available scans

themes.theme: Vendor identified: IDScan.net and its client base

insights.claim: Using publicly available information, Krebs identified IDScan.net, a New Orleans-based ID scanning service, as having an exclusive scanning arrangement with dispensary chain Planet13 and listing Hertz plus 11 other companies as clients; IDScan.net's scans capture both infrared and ultraviolet spectra.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Names the likely breach vector (IDScan.net) and implicated named customers (Hertz, Planet13) — actionable for assessing counterparty/vendor risk if covering these companies or the broader identity-verification vendor space.
insights.locator: Using publicly available information, Krebs found

insights.claim: Neither IDScan.net representatives nor the author's car rental company immediately answered questions about the breach when contacted, though an IDScan.net spokesperson told Krebs the company is investigating.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Lack of prompt vendor response/transparency is a red flag for incident-response quality and potential reputational/liability risk for IDScan.net and its client businesses.
insights.locator: Representatives from IDScan didn't immediately answer

insights.claim: Besides driver's licenses, Nexus also advertised sales of identification cards, travel cards, international DL/ID, medical cards, Common Access Cards (which grant physical access to government buildings and secure rooms), residence cards, employment authorizations, and marijuana dispensary cards, with the FBI investigating.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Exposure of Common Access Cards (CAC), which grant physical access to secure government facilities, elevates this from a consumer-fraud story to a potential national-security concern warranting federal investigation.
insights.quote: government issued identity cards that grant physical access to government buildings and secure rooms
insights.locator: Other records identified the source notation as "CAC,"

insights.claim: Nexus went offline within hours of the KrebsOnSecurity exposé being published, which the author notes is 'somewhat consoling' but also means affected individuals have no way to check if their IDs were included in the breach.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The site's disappearance removes the immediate active marketplace but does not eliminate risk, since already-downloaded/sold ID data can still circulate — highlighting the limits of relying on takedowns alone.
insights.quote: Nexus went dark within hours of the KrebsOnSecurity scoop, although that also means there's no way for people to check if their IDs are included.
